evidence: Liv. 1.4.6: vastae tum in hīs locīs sōlitūdinēs erant (Lewis & Short)
Nep. Att. 1.2: ut tum erant tempora (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The plain word of classical prose. In a series tum also means “next” (see then, next).
Lewis & Short: in classical prose tunc is emphatic (“just then”), and Cicero writes tum about thirty times as often; it becomes common only after Augustus.

evidence: Liv. 6.38.12: eō tempore, quō prōmulgātum dē multā ejus trāditur (Lewis & Short s.v. tempus)

terms.gloss: at that time of day, at that hour
terms.grammar: the neuter id with a genitive, used as an adverb
evidence: Traupman 88: at that time, ad id temporis
terms.comment: Like id aetātis (see age). Traupman's ad id temporis is rather “up to that time”.

sources: Lewis & Short: tum · Lewis & Short: tunc · Lewis & Short: tempus · Lewis & Short: is
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 88, each phrase checked against the searchable text of the book.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
